title: Workers feared AI would kill jobs. Instead, 72% of employers say they’ll pay more for AI skills
source_used: Fortune (fulltext/C14-16.txt, 5,313 chars, HTTP 200); Robert Half press release of 1 Oct 2026 on PR Newswire read for the date and figures (dl14/c16_pr.txt)
key_facts: Robert Half, a talent consulting firm, says over half of employers will offer higher-than-expected salaries to attract new hires in 2027; about 57% of US managers say they are offering higher-than-planned salaries.
About 72% of managers plan to boost pay for recruits with relevant AI skills and 42% say that knowledge commands a greater surcharge than other technical skills.

Dawn Fay, Robert Half's operational president, told Fortune employers will pay more for professionals who understand where AI can add value, integrate it into daily processes and apply it responsibly.
A LinkedIn analysis earlier this year found US AI job postings have doubled since 2023, with the average AI posting offering about $177,000 a year against roughly $80,000 for non-AI roles.
San Francisco and Washington DC are among the cities where most employers are paying more; New York and Chicago are not among the leaders.

Projected 2027 pay rises for new hires include data scientists 3.3%, financial analysts 3.8% and attorneys with four to nine years' experience 3.9%, against 1.7% across all specialties in Fortune's account; about 64% of managers say job offers are more competitive than three years ago.

Fortune sets the data against worker fears: about 60% of white-collar tech workers believe AI could replace their roles within three to five years (Udacity, 2025), and McKinsey Global Institute says AI and automation will cut demand for about 36 million US jobs by 2035 while new growth creates 41 million roles.
An Ipsos study with Google says about 40% of US workers casually use AI at work and 5% are 'AI fluent', who are over four times more likely to report higher earnings and promotions.
quote_evidence: Around 72% of managers plan to boost pay for recruits with relevant AI skills, and 42% say that knowledge commands a greater surcharge than other technical skills.
The average AI job posting offers an annual salary of around $177,000, compared to non-AI roles, which typically pay roughly $80,000.
While AI and automation will cut demand for around 36 million U.S. jobs by 2035, new growth will generate the need for 41 million other roles, according to data from McKinsey Global Institute.
why_it_matters_hint: Employers say they will pay a premium for AI skills, which points to a pay gap between workers who have them and those who do not.
event_date: Robert Half's 2027 Salary Guide was released on 1 Oct 2026; Fortune article 5 Oct 2026.
notes: Older data re-reported: Robert Half published the 2027 Salary Guide on 1 Oct 2026 (PR Newswire), with the same 72%, 42%, 57% and 64% figures; Fortune adds an interview with Dawn Fay and wider context. Fortune's headline says 'employers' but the survey counts managers. Discrepancy: Fortune quotes 1.7% as the average projected rise across specialties, Robert Half's release says 1.9%; neither is used in the summary. Not found in our archived editions 23 Sep to 5 Oct (a different Robert Half study ran on 1 Oct).
